subject_line: Coal mines, demolition derbies and a prayer to the radio
email_body:
Dear Carrie,

After the Revival keeps a real tenderness for things that are run down and wrecked, from abandoned coal mines to demolition derbies, and your poem "The Poet Prays to Her Radio for a Country Song" reads almost like a statement of method for the book. I'd love to ask how country music's plainspoken storytelling shaped your sense of form, and how running Murray State's creative writing program has changed the way you think about those poems now.

book_title: All We Are Given We Cannot Hold
subject_line: From the Professor and Grief to All We Are Given We Cannot Hold
email_body:
Dear Robert,

In Severance you set two puppet-like figures, the Professor and Grief, moving toward something like healing, and All We Are Given We Cannot Hold, your Dzanc collection, turns to love, family and elegies for your mother. I'm curious how writing grief directly differs from staging it through those invented figures, and how hosting the Wellspring Literary Series in Mt. Pleasant feeds your own work.

subject_line: Pearls, open windows and Ella's Plan
email_body:
Dear Jeffrey,

Your titles keep returning to the act of looking at a painting: Girl Reading a Letter at an Open Window, then Woman Putting on Pearls, which won the Red Mountain Prize, and later The Voyeur's Litany. I'd love to ask what draws you to writing from inside a fixed, framed scene, and how Ella's Plan, the chapbook Naomi Shihab Nye chose for The Poets Corner prize, moves away from or toward that habit.

In your Southern Review of Books conversation about To Make Room for the Sea, you described starting the collection with your daughter and the Anthropocene in mind, then watching the poems change as your marriage ended while you finalized the manuscript. I'd like to ask what Circle Back, your newer Milkweed book, inherited from that shift, and whether forms like the sestina and abecedarian still feel like the right containers for hope.

book_title: All the Places We Love Have Been Left in Ruins
subject_line: Mourning a Miami that is already being lost
email_body:
Dear Ariel,

All the Places We Love Have Been Left in Ruins grieves a Miami already damaged by climate change and development, and it reads differently knowing you grew up there after being born in the Bronx to Dominican and Guatemalan parents. In The Rumpus you explained that you focus your translations on poets from the Dominican Republic and Guatemala because they are your parents' home countries. I'd love to ask how writing from Louisiana now changes the way you look back at Miami.

book_title: God, the Moon, and Other Megafauna
subject_line: Midwestern magical realism, from Fat Girl, Terrestrial to the megafauna
email_body:
Dear Kellie,

Years ago, in a University of Montana profile, you called your approach "Midwestern magical-realism" and described writing slowly, paragraph by paragraph. That phrase still seems to fit the line running from Compression Scars and Fat Girl, Terrestrial to God, the Moon, and Other Megafauna. I'd love to ask whether the label still feels right to you after many years in Alabama, and what the story form allows the strange that a novel doesn't.

subject_line: Too far or not far enough: a question about Off Message
email_body:
Dear Joel,

In your Ploughshares interview about And So, you said every poem you'd written seemed to you either to have gone too far or not far enough. I've been wondering how that feeling applied to Off Message, your Four Way Books collection, whose title suggests a poet deliberately straying from the script. I'd like to ask how you judge when a poem has reached the right distance, and whether teaching criticism in Tuscaloosa has changed that judgment.

subject_line: From a Waseca graveyard to Camilla Hall
email_body:
Dear Rachael,

Your memoir We'll Be the Last Ones to Let You Down grew out of a childhood as a gravedigger's daughter in Waseca, gathering stories among the headstones, and Not the Camilla We Knew turns that same attentiveness toward Camilla Hall and her path into the Symbionese Liberation Army. I'd love to ask how reconstructing a stranger's life differed from excavating your own, and what you hoped readers would understand about her that the headlines never did.

book_title: I'm Sorry You Feel That Way
subject_line: The title I'm Sorry You Feel That Way, and the essay "The Boy"
email_body:
Dear Diana,

I'm Sorry You Feel That Way borrows its title from the most familiar non-apology there is, which feels like a sly promise about the candor and comedy of the memoir that follows. Your essay "The Boy" also won the Kentucky Women Writers Prize for Creative Nonfiction. Coming to nonfiction after the stories in Happy or Otherwise, how did you decide how much of yourself to put on the page, and what do you tell Mankato MFA students about that line?

subject_line: Round Baby, the girl-alien of Mostly Human
email_body:
Dear Sheila,

Round Baby, the girl-alien who carries Mostly Human through the 1980s, adolescence, sexuality and gender roles, is such an inventive way to come at experience that, as you told The Rumpus, rises right out of your own life. I'd love to ask how an alien persona gave you permission to say things a plain first person couldn't, and whether Round Baby has followed you into anything you've written since the Wicked Woman Book Prize.

subject_line: Calamity, comfort and the title People You May Know
email_body:
Dear Michael,

People You May Know has a title that sounds like a social media prompt, yet the poems themselves move through loss and grief toward something like comfort and renewal, rising out of calamity and failure. That follows In Memory of Brilliance & Value, where your couplets set grazing buffalo beside torture and war. I'd love to ask what you carried forward from those couplets, and how moving from Chicago to teach at McNeese in Lake Charles has entered the newer work.

book_title: Others Will Enter the Gates: Immigrant Poets on Poetry, Influences, and Writing in America
subject_line: Immigrant poets at the gates, from The Giving of Pears to Seahorses
email_body:
Dear Abayomi,

You've built a body of work in two directions at once: your own collections, from The Giving of Pears, which won the Hudson Prize, through Sailing for Ithaca and Seahorses, and anthologies like Others Will Enter the Gates, which gathers immigrant poets reflecting on influence and on writing in America. I'd love to ask how editing those voices has shaped your own poems as a Nigerian-born poet living in Green Bay, and what newer poets most often ask you about belonging.

subject_line: A convent in Italy, begun on a train to Shanghai
email_body:
Dear Liam,

You told Milwaukee Magazine that the prologue of When in Rome was written on a bullet train from Beijing to Shanghai in 2018, which is a long way from the struggling Italian convent the novel's American heroine sets out to save. I'd love to ask how that unlikely starting point fed a story about beginning again at midlife, and how it sits beside Paris by the Book and the moments of sudden change you explored in the stories of Listen.

subject_line: Charlie Brown, Cher, Casablanca and the art of the flash title
email_body:

I'd love to ask why celebrity works so well as a compressed setting, and what directing Ball State's creative writing program has taught you about teaching the very short form.
